items.q: Match the following thyroiditis phase to its expected TFT pattern — 1) Hyperthyroid phase 2) Hypothyroid phase 3) Recovery … A) ↑FT4, ↓TSH, low uptake, raised ESR B) ↓FT4, ↑TSH, low uptake C) Normal TFTs and ESR
items.exp: Hyperthyroid phase has high free T4/T3 with low TSH and raised ESR; hypothyroid phase has low free hormone with high TSH; recovery normalises both TFTs and ESR. (Book p915)

items.q: An outpatient with subacute thyroiditis at week 6 still has fatigue, weight gain and a TSH of 12 mIU/L. The most appropriate therapy is:
opts: Levothyroxine replacement during the hypothyroid phase
items.exp: The hypothyroid phase is treated with levothyroxine; thionamides are ineffective because hormone is not being synthesised. (Book p915)

items.q: Assess postpartum thyroiditis: I Anti-TPO antibodies predict higher risk. II Permanent hypothyroidism develops in a minority.
items.exp: Anti-TPO positivity predicts postpartum thyroiditis; permanent hypothyroidism develops in roughly 20–30% of affected women. (Book p915)

items.q: Which is the odd one out — a feature of subacute thyroiditis (de Quervain)?
opts: Diffuse painless goitre without ESR rise
items.exp: Painless goitre without ESR rise fits painless/postpartum thyroiditis rather than the painful de Quervain subacute variant. (Book p915)

items.q: Pain in subacute thyroiditis typically responds to ___; corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases.
items.exp: NSAIDs are first-line analgesia; corticosteroids are added in severe or refractory cases. (Book p915)

items.q: Match the following graph feature — 1) X-axis 2) Y-axes (left/right) 3) Toxic phase timing … A) Time (weeks from onset) B) UT4 (left) and ESR (right) C) Weeks 0–4 typically thyrotoxic
items.exp: The schematic plots time in weeks on the x-axis; UT4 (free T4) and ESR appear on the y-axes; the toxic phase occupies weeks 0–4 of illness. (Book p915)

items.q: At week 8 of subacute thyroiditis, the patient has normal free T4 and normal ESR. The best next step is:
opts: Continue to monitor with periodic TFTs
items.exp: Recovery normalises TFTs and ESR; further observation without specific therapy is appropriate, with follow-up for late hypothyroidism. (Book p915)

items.q: Assess these statements: I Corticosteroids shorten painful phase but do not prevent hypothyroidism. II Subacute thyroiditis always recurs.
items.exp: Corticosteroids ease symptoms without altering the natural biphasic course; recurrence is uncommon though possible. (Book p915)

items.q: Match the following postpartum thyroiditis finding to its prevalence — 1) Anti-TPO positive 2) Symptomatic thyroid dysfunction 3) Permanent hypothyroidism … A) ~50% of women who develop it B) Up to 5–10% of pregnancies C) ~20–30% of cases
items.exp: Among women with postpartum thyroiditis, about half are anti-TPO positive; symptomatic disease occurs in 5–10% of pregnancies; permanent hypothyroidism develops in ~20–30% of cases. (Book p915)

items.q: A 32-year-old with postpartum thyroiditis asks about future pregnancies. Which statement is most consistent with the source?
opts: Recurrence risk is high in subsequent pregnancies
items.exp: Recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is common; permanent hypothyroidism is possible but not inevitable. (Book p915)

items.q: Recurrent subacute thyroiditis occurs in roughly ___% of patients.
items.exp: Recurrence after de Quervain thyroiditis is uncommon, around 1–4% in published series; the page emphasises the typically self-limiting nature. (Book p915)

items.q: Assess these caveats: I Postpartum thyroiditis can be mistaken for Graves disease initially. II Both disorders show low uptake on scan.
items.exp: Postpartum thyroiditis can mimic Graves early, but Graves shows high uptake whereas postpartum thyroiditis shows low uptake. (Book p915)
